Hardy's inequality

Words: 29
Real analysis OurBigBook.com
Hardy's inequality bounds averages or weighted functions by their original size or derivatives. For p>1 and f≥0, its integral form is ∫0∞​(x−1∫0x​f(t)dt)pdx≤(p/(p−1))p∫0∞​f(x)pdx. Spatial weighted forms include the Hardy inequality in Euclidean space.

Infimum and supremum (inf, sup)

Words: 203 Articles: 5
Real analysis OurBigBook.com
The infimum of a subset of an ordered set is its greatest lower bound; its supremum is its least upper bound. Neither bound must belong to the subset. For bounded nonempty subsets of the real numbers both bounds exist by completeness of the real numbers.

Essential infimum and essential supremum (essinf, esssup)

Words: 67 Articles: 1
Infimum and supremum OurBigBook.com
The essential bounds disregard null sets. For a real measurable function f, its essential supremum is inf{a:f≤a almost everywhere} and its essential infimum is sup{a:f≥a almost everywhere}. Unlike pointwise infimum and supremum, these values are unchanged by changing f on a null set.

Essential infimum (essinfu)

Words: 29
Essential infimum and essential supremum OurBigBook.com
The essential infimum of a measurable function is essinfu=−esssup(−u). It is the largest lower bound that holds almost everywhere. Unlike a pointwise infimum, it is unchanged by altering a representative on a null set.

Supremum (sup)

Words: 84 Articles: 1
Infimum and supremum OurBigBook.com
The supremum of a set of real numbers is its least upper bound.

Accumulation below an unattained supremum

Words: 71
Supremum OurBigBook.com
If a nonempty real set A has finite supremum s and s∈/A, then every interval (s−ε,s) contains infinitely many elements of A. Otherwise its finitely many elements have a largest value m<s; all remaining elements are at most s−ε, making max(m,s−ε)<s an upper bound. The interval cannot be empty either, by the defining approximation property of a supremum. Thus failure to attain a finite supremum forces accumulation from below.

The infimum of a set of real numbers is its greatest lower bound.

Stirling correction by Gaussian moments (Γ(x)∼2π​xx−1/2e−x(1+1/(12x)))
Words: 50
Stirling formula OurBigBook.com
In Laplace method for the Gamma function, scaling t=x(1+s/x​) gives a standard Gaussian integral. The first even correction polynomial is s2−7s4/12+s6/18. Its expectation under a unit-variance centered Gaussian is 1−7⋅3/12+15/18=1/12. The amplitude expansion contributes to this coefficient as well as the phase expansion; expanding only the latter gives the wrong Stirling formula correction.

Monotone integral Tauberian lemma (∫1∞​(β(x)−x)x−2dx converges ⟹ β(x)/x→1)

Words: 71
Real analysis OurBigBook.com
For nondecreasing real β, convergence of the displayed improper integral forces β(x)/x→1. For λ>1, the integral over [X,λX] tends to zero and is at least (1−λ−1)β(X)/X−logλ. The integral over [X/λ,X] tends to zero and is at most (λ−1)β(X)/X−logλ. These bound the upper and lower limits by logλ/(1−λ−1) and logλ/(λ−1). Letting λ↓1 squeezes both to one. The limit of the improper integral must be finite.

Homogeneous function (f(λx)=λkf(x))

Words: 374 Articles: 5
Real analysis OurBigBook.com
A function is homogeneous of degree k when rescaling its arguments by a common scalar λ rescales its value by λk, whenever the arguments and that power are defined. For integer k over a vector space, one can require every nonzero scalar; a homogeneous polynomial gives an example. On a domain stable under positive real rescaling, the positive-scaling version allows real k. Degree-one positive homogeneity is the convention used for norms and many convex functions. The Euler theorem for homogeneous functions turns this scaling law into a differential identity for a differentiable function.

Homogeneity (f(ax)=akf(x))

Words: 42
Homogeneous function OurBigBook.com
Homogeneity of degree k means that multiplying all arguments by a common positive factor a multiplies the output by ak. A homogeneous function is the function possessing this property. This is different from degree-one positive homogeneity; investment values with constant relative risk aversion utility usually have degree 1−R.

Positively homogeneous function (degree one)

Words: 38
Homogeneous function OurBigBook.com
A function on a cone is positively homogeneous of degree one when f(tX)=tf(X) for every t>0. If such a function is concave, then
f(X+tY)≥f(X)+tf(Y),
(1)
because homogeneity rewrites the left-hand side as (1+t)f((X+tY)/(1+t)) before concavity is applied.

Euler theorem for homogeneous functions (∑i​xi​∂i​f=kf)

Words: 214 Articles: 2
Homogeneous function OurBigBook.com
Let f be a differentiable function on an open domain stable under positive rescaling, with f(λx)=λkf(x) for λ>0. The chain rule differentiates this homogeneous function identity at λ=1 to give
∑i​xi​∂i​f(x)=kf(x).
(2)
If f is twice differentiable, differentiating once more gives ∑i​xi​∂i​∂j​f=(k−1)∂j​f. In degree one its Hessian matrix therefore annihilates the radial vector x. This is the identity used in the no-scale identity from degree-one homogeneity. For an extensive quantity, the degree-one formula also supplies the thermodynamic identity behind the Gibbs-Duhem equation.

Euler differential identity characterizes homogeneity

Words: 46
Euler theorem for homogeneous functions OurBigBook.com
On an open domain invariant under positive scaling, Dfx​(x)=cf(x) implies f(λx)=λcf(x). Indeed, dλd​[λ−cf(λx)]=λ−c−1[Dfλx​(λx)−cf(λx)]=0. The converse follows by differentiating the scaling identity at λ=1. Connectedness of the whole domain is unnecessary: the argument works along each positive ray.

Volume integral of a homogeneous function (∫V​fdV=n+31​∫∂V​fx⋅ndS)

Words: 93
Euler theorem for homogeneous functions OurBigBook.com
For a sufficiently regular homogeneous function f of degree n on a three-dimensional region, Euler theorem for homogeneous functions gives x⋅∇f=nf. Hence ∇⋅(fx)=(n+3)f, and the divergence theorem gives the displayed reduction when n=−3. At degree −3 only the zero-flux identity follows, so division by n+3 is unavailable. Singular functions additionally require an excision or limiting argument; the surface contribution at a removed singularity must not be silently dropped. On the sloping side of a cone with its apex at zero, x is tangent to the side and x⋅n=0, so only the cap contributes to this formula.

Real analysis OurBigBook.com
A positive measurable function q has regular variation at infinity with index ρ if q(tu)/q(t)→uρ for every u>0. Equivalently, q(t)=tρℓ(t) with ℓ a slowly varying function.

Slowly varying function

Regular variation OurBigBook.com
A slowly varying function has regular variation with index zero: ℓ(tu)/ℓ(t)→1 for every u>0. A power of logt is an example.

Lipschitz continuity

Words: 405 Articles: 10
Real analysis OurBigBook.com
A function f is Lipschitz continuous when there is a constant L≥0 such that
∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤L∣x−y∣
(3)
for all points in its domain.

Bounded Lipschitz norm (∥f∥BL​=supx=y​∣f(x)−f(y)∣/d(x,y)+supz​∣f(z)∣)

Words: 145 Articles: 2
Lipschitz continuity OurBigBook.com
The bounded Lipschitz norm combines the Lipschitz constant and supremum norm of a bounded real-valued Lipschitz function on a metric space. Both summands satisfy the triangle inequality; the supremum term makes the sum definite even on constant functions. Its unit ball requires the sum of the two bounds to be at most one, a stronger requirement than bounding each separately by one.

Diagonal compactness for bounded Lipschitz functions

Words: 47
Bounded Lipschitz norm OurBigBook.com
On a separable metric space, a sequence uniformly bounded in bounded Lipschitz norm has a pointwise convergent subsequence. Enumerate a countable dense subset and use the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem and diagonal subsequence argument to obtain convergence there. Uniform control of the Lipschitz constant then makes the subsequence Cauchy at every point. The pointwise closure of the bounded Lipschitz unit ball preserves the original norm bound after rescaling.

Pointwise closure of the bounded Lipschitz unit ball (fi​→f pointwise,∥fi​∥BL​≤1 ⟹ ∥f∥BL​≤1)

Words: 44
Bounded Lipschitz norm OurBigBook.com
For every fixed x=y and z, the sum ∣fi​(x)−fi​(y)∣/d(x,y)+∣fi​(z)∣ is at most one. Pointwise convergence preserves this inequality. Taking the independent suprema over the pair (x,y) and the point z proves the assertion. Taking each bound separately would only give the weaker estimate two.

One-sided Lipschitz condition (Re⟨f(y)−f(z),y−z⟩≤ν∥y−z∥2)

Words: 54
Lipschitz continuity OurBigBook.com
A one-sided Lipschitz condition controls the growth of distances between solutions of an ordinary differential equation. Differentiating the squared difference and applying the Gronwall inequality gives ∥y(t)−z(t)∥≤eνt∥y(0)−z(0)∥. The case ν≤0 is a dissipative vector field. Ordinary Lipschitz continuity implies such a bound, but the converse fails: f(y)=−y3 has one-sided constant zero on the real line without being globally Lipschitz continuous.

Lipschitz domain

Words: 60
Lipschitz continuity OurBigBook.com
A Lipschitz domain is an open connected subset of Euclidean space whose boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz continuous function after rotating and translating coordinates. Locally the domain lies on one side of that graph. This permits corners but excludes boundary cusps that cannot be represented with a finite Lipschitz constant. Bounded Lipschitz domains are a standard setting for Sobolev spaces and the Poincaré inequality for total variation.

McShane extension theorem

Words: 26
Lipschitz continuity OurBigBook.com
If f:A→R is L-Lipschitz on a subset of a metric space, then
F(x)=infy∈A​{f(y)+Ld(x,y)}
(4)
extends f to the whole space and remains L-Lipschitz.

Lipschitz constant (L)

Words: 21
Lipschitz continuity OurBigBook.com
The least L≥0 for which d(f(x),f(y))≤Ld(x,y) for every x,y is the Lipschitz constant of f. Any admissible L is a Lipschitz bound.

Globally Lipschitz function

Words: 31
Lipschitz continuity OurBigBook.com
A function is globally Lipschitz when one Lipschitz bound holds for every pair of points in its domain. Unlike local Lipschitz continuity, this condition gives a uniform growth control over the whole domain.

Lipschitz bound

A Lipschitz bound has the form ∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤L∣x−y∣. It controls the change of a function by the change of its argument.

Locally Lipschitz function

A function is locally Lipschitz when every point has a neighborhood on which the function satisfies a Lipschitz bound. Continuously differentiable functions are locally Lipschitz.

Sequence OurBigBook.com
Two bounded real sequences with the same set of subsequential limits admit permutations that match their terms with differences tending to zero. Changing the value of a bounded Riemann-integrable function at one point preserves its Riemann integral. The weak Euler-Lagrange equation is divDF(Du)=0. Difference quotients solve uniformly elliptic equations with coefficient matrices obtained by averaging D2F along gradient segments. The Caccioppoli inequality and difference quotient characterization give u∈Hloc2​. The Sobolev chain rule then gives div(D2F(Du)D(Dk​u))=0. The De Giorgi-Nash-Moser theorem makes each derivative Hölder continuous, with exponent depending only on dimension and the ellipticity ratio. This scalar conclusion should not be assumed for vector-valued elliptic systems.

The coefficients are uniformly elliptic and locally smooth. Apply the weak maximum principle on inner domains whose closures lie in the original domain, then let their boundary distances tend to zero. The common continuous boundary values make their boundary differences tend uniformly to zero, proving uniqueness without assuming global bounds on derivatives of the linearized coefficients.

For 0<c<1 on the probability simplex, xic​≥xi​ gives the lower bound, with equality exactly at its vertices. Let a differentiable concave function on all of Rd be strictly increasing in each coordinate separately. Every coordinate derivative is strictly positive. Indeed it is nonnegative by monotonicity and nonincreasing along its coordinate by concavity; a zero value would force zero derivative on the remaining positive ray and hence a constant segment. The global-domain assumption matters at endpoints of restricted domains.

For a differentiable concave function, secant slopes lie below the tangent slope at their left endpoint and above the tangent slope at their right endpoint. Positive-product maximization on a convex set
Words: 71
Strict concavity OurBigBook.com
A compact convex subset of R2 meeting the positive quadrant has a unique positive point maximizing xy. Existence follows by maximizing the continuous product on the intersection with the closed nonnegative quadrant; a positive attainable value excludes its axes. Uniqueness follows from strict concavity of logx+logy on the positive quadrant. This is a useful way to optimize a product even though the product itself is not concave.

Uniform negative curvature and global maximization (f′′(x)≤−c<0)

Words: 86
Strictly concave function OurBigBook.com
If a twice differentiable real function on R satisfies f′′(x)≤−c for some fixed c>0, then it has a unique global maximum. The mean value theorem shows that f′ is strictly decreasing, and that f′(x)+cx is nonincreasing. Hence f′(x)≤f′(0)−cx for x>0 and f′(x)≥f′(0)−cx for x<0. These inequalities force opposite derivative signs at the two ends. The intermediate value theorem supplies a unique zero of f′, at which f changes from increasing to decreasing. Merely having f′′<0 does not guarantee existence: f(x)=−e−x is increasing and approaches its unattained supremum zero.
